entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Very rich. The Library holds 106 of his own works on the shelf of the Latin Pastoral Congregations: sermons, letters, treatises, and the Confessions. Possidius, his friend and fellow bishop, wrote his Life.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He wrote On the Trinity and stood with the Nicene faith.
entries.relationsSummary: He is told within the Latin Pastoral Congregations, as their bishop at Hippo. For many years he argued with the Manichaeans and the Donatists. Then he took on the followers of Pelagius.
entries.why: Augustine is the most fully recorded pastor of the ancient world. A teacher of rhetoric, he came to faith in a garden in Milan in 386. He then served one African town as priest and bishop until he died there in 430, with the Vandals at its walls.
entries.teaser: Hippo Regius, 386 to 430 CE: a teacher of rhetoric who became a bishop. He preached to one African town for most of his life, and argued with half the Christian world.
entries.longDescription:
Augustine was born at Tagaste in 354. From his nineteenth year he followed the Manichaeans for nine years. He taught rhetoric at Carthage, and then at Rome and Milan. In Milan he went to hear Ambrose preach. In September 386 he sat in the garden of the house where he lodged in Milan. A child's voice from a nearby house chanted 'Take up and read', and he turned to Christ. Ambrose baptized him at Easter 387.

Back in Africa, the people of Hippo Regius made him a priest in 391, against his will. In 395 he became bishop there. He stayed in that town for the rest of his life.

Much of his writing was argument. He answered the Manichaeans he had once joined, among them their teacher Faustus. He argued for years with the Donatist church that stood beside his own, and met its bishops at Carthage in 411. Later he wrote against Pelagius on grace and human nature. Julian of Eclanum called the Catholic party Manichaeans, and Augustine answered him in four books.

After the Goths sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed the Christians for the disaster. In 413 Augustine began the City of God in answer, and he finished it in 426. He died at Hippo on 28 August 430, in the third month of the Vandal siege.
voices: Augustine of Hippo — bishop of Hippo Regius for thirty-five years, and the most extensively documented working pastor of the ancient world
Possidius of Calama — Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, who wrote his biography and cataloged his works
entries.legacy: Later churches kept coming back to him. Around 550, Facundus of Hermiane called him the 'most wise and most famous teacher of the churches of Christ'. In Geneva, Calvin wrote that he could fill a whole book with Augustine's words alone. Port-Royal took its view of grace from him, and Cornelius Jansen named his own book Augustinus. Rome condemned five propositions said to come from that book in 1653. People still argue over what Augustine taught on grace.

entries.name: Cyprian of Carthage
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 35 of his own works on the shelf of the Latin Pastoral Congregations: letters and treatises in Latin, French and English, and the Life by his deacon Pontius.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. His quarrel with Rome was over baptism given outside the church, not over the faith itself.
entries.relationsSummary: He is told within the Latin Pastoral Congregations, as bishop of Carthage. He refused to take in Novatian's envoys. He argued with Stephen of Rome over baptism. Later the Donatists quoted him to defend their own break.
entries.why: Cyprian led the church of Carthage through persecution, plague and schism, and his letters are the fullest record of how a third-century church was run. He read Tertullian every day and called him 'the master'.
entries.teaser: Carthage, 248 to 258 CE: a teacher of rhetoric made bishop two years after his baptism. He held his church together by letter, and he died by the sword.
entries.longDescription:
Cyprian was trained as a rhetorician and became a Christian around 246. Two years later the people of Carthage pressed him to become their bishop. Some older presbyters objected. He held the office until his death in 258.

When Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice in 250, Cyprian went into hiding. The clergy of Rome attacked him for it in a letter. From his hiding place he kept running his church by letter. Many of his people had sacrificed, and he had to decide how to take them back.

When plague struck, he gathered his people and preached on mercy. It was nothing great, he said, to care only for their own. God sends sun and rain to all, and a child of God should do the same.

He fought hard for the unity of the church. 'He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother,' he wrote. He refused the envoys of Novatian, a rival bishop at Rome. In 255 he and a council of African bishops told Stephen of Rome that people coming from heresy must be baptized. Stephen disagreed, and Cyprian called it his error.

Under Valerian he was arrested and beheaded outside Carthage in 258. The crowd was so large that some climbed the trees to watch.
voices: Cyprian of Carthage — bishop through persecution and plague, whose letters are the fullest surviving picture of how a third-century congregation actually ran
Pontius the Deacon — Cyprian's deacon, who wrote an account of his bishop's life and death
entries.legacy: Both sides of a later split claimed him. The Donatists kept quoting his letters and his council to defend their break. Augustine asked them why. Augustine himself said Cyprian was wrong about baptism. But he never doubted the man. Around 550, Facundus still cited 'blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr'. In 533, Procopius reports, the people of Carthage loved Cyprian above all other holy men.

entries.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Moderate. Against Heresies survives whole in Latin and English, and fragments of his lost writings survive too. Both sit on the Household-Church shelf. Most of what is known of his life comes from Eusebius.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He wrote more than a century before the Nicene Creed.
entries.relationsSummary: He is told within the Household Churches of the years after the apostles. He wrote against the Valentinians and Marcion. He also listed Rome's bishops, to show where the apostles' teaching was kept.
entries.why: As a boy Irenaeus saw Polycarp of Smyrna. Later he led the church at Lyon in Gaul. His five books Against Heresies are the fullest answer to the Valentinians that we still have. He wrote them while Eleutherius was bishop of Rome.
entries.teaser: Lyon, c. 177 to 190 CE: a bishop who had seen Polycarp as a boy, answering the Valentinians by asking which churches the apostles had taught.
entries.longDescription:
As a boy, Irenaeus saw Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, who had been taught by apostles. Later he wrote that Polycarp always taught what he had learned from the apostles.

Around 177 the Christians of Lyon in Gaul were in prison, awaiting death. They wrote to Eleutherius, bishop of Rome, and asked Irenaeus to carry the letter. They called him 'zealous for the covenant of Christ', a presbyter of their church. Their bishop Pothinus died with the martyrs, and Irenaeus took his place.

His great work, Against Heresies, was written while Eleutherius led the church of Rome. It sets out the teaching of the Valentinians and answers it at length. He named the bishops of Rome in order, from the apostles down to Eleutherius, who 'does now' hold the office. Polycarp, he adds, turned many at Rome away from the followers of Valentinus and Marcion.

Later, Victor of Rome threatened to cut off the churches of Asia over the date of Easter. Irenaeus wrote for the churches of Gaul. He held that Easter belonged on the Lord's day, but he warned Victor not to cut off whole churches for keeping an ancient custom.
voices: Irenaeus of Lyon — presbyter and then bishop of Lyon, who had heard Polycarp in his youth and wrote the five books Against Heresies
The martyrs of Lyon and Vienne — the imprisoned Christians who sent him to Rome with their letter, around 177
entries.legacy: His list of Rome's bishops became a starting point for later arguments about who holds the apostles' teaching. Historians still weigh it. Peter Lampe argues that Rome had no single bishop in charge until about 189 to 199. His account of the Valentinians and of Marcion remains a main witness to both, but it is the witness of an opponent.

entries.name: Jovinian
entries.statusDescription: Everything known about him comes from the bishops who condemned him and the scholar who answered him. None of his own writing survives except where they quote it.
entries.sourcing: Thin and hostile. His own book is lost. Jerome quotes its main points in his two books Against Jovinianus, and a letter of Ambrose warns against two monks his editor takes for Jovinian's followers.
entries.floorNote: Not a Creed question, as far as the record goes. The points that were condemned are about virginity, marriage, fasting, sin after baptism and reward in heaven. Only his opponents report them.
entries.relationsSummary: Known only through Jerome and Ambrose, who both wrote against him. Their editors report that synods at Rome and Milan condemned his book about 390.
entries.why: Jovinian taught that a baptized wife is no lower in God's sight than a virgin, and that fasting is no better than eating with thanks. Rome and Milan condemned him, and Jerome answered him in two long books.
entries.teaser: Rome, c. 390 CE: a monk who put off the monk's dress and said marriage was as good as virginity, known only from the men who condemned him.
entries.longDescription:
Jovinian is known only through Jerome and Ambrose. No tradition on this map tells his story, and none of his own writing survives whole. What remains is what his opponents chose to quote.

Jerome's editor calls him a Roman monk, or rather a solitary, who put off the monk's dress and lived like other men. He wrote a book in Latin at Rome. Jerome quotes four points from it. Baptized virgins, widows and wives are of equal merit. Those reborn in baptism with full faith cannot be overthrown by the devil. Fasting is no better than eating with thanks. And all who keep their baptismal vow share one reward in heaven.

Pammachius, a friend of Jerome, brought the book to Siricius, bishop of Rome. By the editors' account, synods at Rome and at Milan condemned it about 390. Ambrose and his synod wrote back to Siricius to join the sentence. In a letter to the church at Vercelli, Ambrose warned against two monks who said there is 'no merit in abstinence' and none in virginity. His editor takes them for followers of Jovinian.

In 393 Jerome answered the book with two books of his own, Against Jovinianus. He calls Jovinian 'the Epicurus of Christianity'. Even Jerome's editor gives a warning here. He says Jerome's charges about the man's life are guesses drawn from his views. They are not known facts.
voices: Jovinian — a Roman monk whose book is lost; his four main points survive only as Jerome quotes them
Jerome — who answered him in two books Against Jovinianus in 393
Ambrose of Milan — whose synod joined the sentence passed on him at Rome
entries.legacy: His book is lost, and his side lost the argument. Jerome's reply survives. Jerome himself later wrote to Pammachius that some thought he had gone too far in those books, praising virginity and running down marriage.

entries.name: Ambrose of Milan
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich for one bishop. The Library holds nine of his own works on the shelf of Ambrose's Milan, including his letters, with the Life written by Paulinus of Milan.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He was a leading defender of the Nicene faith against the Homoian bishops.
entries.relationsSummary: He is told within Ambrose's Milan, the city church he led as bishop. He argued with the court, with the Homoian bishops and with Priscillian. His synod joined the sentence on Jovinian, and he baptized Augustine.
entries.why: Ambrose was still a catechumen when the people of Milan acclaimed him bishop in 374. For twenty-three years he told emperors where their power stopped. He died in his city on Good Friday night, 397.
entries.teaser: Milan, 374 to 397 CE: a man not yet baptized whom a crowd made bishop. He taught emperors that they stood within the church, not above it.
entries.longDescription:
His father held high office in Gaul, and Ambrose was most likely born at Trier, around 340. In 374 Auxentius, the Homoian bishop of Milan, died. The people acclaimed Ambrose as bishop, though he was still a catechumen. He was baptized, and on 7 December 374 he was consecrated.

He argued in public with power. At Aquileia in 381 he questioned the Homoian bishop Palladius. In 386 he preached against Auxentius, a rival bishop, and declared him cast out. 'The Emperor is within the Church, not above it,' he said. In 388 he would not go to the altar until Theodosius dropped a case over a burned synagogue. After the massacre at Thessalonica in 390, he wrote that he dared not offer the sacrifice with the emperor present.

He also judged teachers. About 390, by his editor's account, he and a synod at Milan joined Rome's sentence on the monk Jovinian. In a letter to Vercelli he attacked two monks who said there is 'no merit in abstinence'.

He was also a preacher. Augustine, then a teacher of rhetoric, came to hear him. He wrote that he was led to Ambrose so that Ambrose might lead him to God. Ambrose baptized him at Easter 387.

He died on Good Friday night, 4 to 5 April 397. He was buried on Easter morning in his basilica at Milan.
voices: Ambrose — the governor turned bishop, hymn-writer, and the first churchman to make an emperor do public penance
Paulinus of Milan — who wrote his Life
entries.legacy: Milan still keeps the rite that bears his name, though how much of it goes back to him is unclear. His rule that a Christian emperor stands within the church, not above it, was his lasting word to power. And by Augustine's own account, Ambrose's preaching helped bring Augustine to God.

entries.name: Jerome
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Very rich, and nearly all in his own hand. The Library holds 17 of his own works on the Bethlehem Circle shelf: letters, lives, treatises and his catalog of Christian writers.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He was a combative defender of the Nicene faith.
entries.relationsSummary: He is told within the Bethlehem Circle. He served it as teacher and translator. He broke with Rufinus over Origen. He wrote to Augustine for years, and he attacked Jovinian.
entries.why: Jerome put the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew at Bethlehem, in the work later called the Vulgate. His letters are also the main record of the Roman women who funded that life and shared it.
entries.teaser: Rome and Bethlehem, 374 to 420 CE: a brilliant and quarrelsome scholar who gave the Latin West its Bible from the Hebrew.
entries.longDescription:
Jerome was born at Stridon around 345, and he studied at Rome, where he was baptized. From 374 to 379 he lived in the desert of Chalcis. He wrote from 'the corner of the desert' between the Syrians and the Saracens. From the East he wrote to Damasus of Rome that he kept communion only with 'the chair of Peter'.

From 382 to 385 he was at Rome, helping Damasus with his church letters. Damasus died in 384, and the next year Jerome left the city. In 386 he settled at Bethlehem.

There, from 391, he worked on a Latin Old Testament made from the Hebrew. Augustine urged him to translate from the Greek of the Seventy instead. Jerome kept to the Hebrew. In 393 he wrote two books against Jovinian.

He quarreled as hard as he wrote. He called Origen's teachings poisonous, and around 400 he broke for good with his old friend Rufinus over Origen. He died at Bethlehem on 20 September 420.
voices: Jerome — the scholar and translator at the center of the Bethlehem Circle, whose letters carry nearly everything known of it
Rufinus of Aquileia — his friend from student days, and later his bitter opponent over Origen
entries.legacy: His Latin Bible became the West's standard text, and in 1546 the Council of Trent declared the Vulgate authentic. His catalog, On Illustrious Men, keeps much of what is known about early Christian writers. It is how we know that Cyprian called Tertullian 'the master'.

set.longDescription:
This is the congregational life of Latin-speaking North Africa. It is the week in, week out work of a bishop with a flock, and the hard disputes that pressed on that work. Cyprian became bishop of Carthage around 248. When the emperor Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice, he went into hiding. He came back to the hardest pastoral problem of the age. Thousands of his own people had complied, and now they wanted back in.

He organized relief through the plague that still bears his name. He told his congregation to nurse pagan neighbors as well as their own. He refused communion to the envoys of Novatian, a rival bishop at Rome. He argued with Stephen of Rome over baptism given outside the church. He was beheaded outside Carthage in 258.

A century and a half later, Augustine was bishop of Hippo Regius from 395 until his death in 430. He preached to the same congregation several times a week for thirty-five years, and stenographers took much of it down. Hundreds of those sermons survive. They argue, joke, scold and console actual people whose lives he knew.

His pastoral work ran through the great disputes of his day. A rival Donatist church stood in the same towns, and he argued with it for decades. He answered the Manichaeans, whom he had followed for nine years in his youth. In his last years he wrote against Pelagius and his followers on grace and human nature.

Between the two bishops lay the ordinary round. Catechumens were taught, and new believers were baptized at Easter. Penitents did public penance. The church cared for widows and the poor. And the bishop sat as judge in his own people's disputes.

The old opening 'not the councils and not the controversies' is replaced; the controversies are named as pressing on the pastoral work, and Cyprian's quarrels with Novatian and Stephen are added, each with a link. The text is also split into short paragraphs to meet the reading target. Every other sentence keeps its existing substance. Census field only; the lpc world's files are not touched.

voices: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters to congregations while he was marched toward Rome under armed guard, c. 107-117. Polycarp's own letter later speaks of him as already dead, though it admits not knowing the details of what happened.

Clement of Rome wrote on behalf of the Roman church to the Corinthians around the year 96, addressing a dispute over deposed leaders. The letter is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament to survive.

Polycarp of Smyrna was addressed as bishop by Ignatius, though his own letter never claims the title, opening only as 'Polycarp, and the presbyters with him.' He was put to death at Smyrna around 155; his own congregation recorded his death.
Justin Martyr was a philosopher who kept teaching Christianity as a school in Rome. He left the earliest detailed description of what their Sunday actually looked like.

Irenaeus had seen Polycarp at Smyrna as a boy, and later led the church at Lyon in Gaul. While Eleutherius was bishop of Rome he wrote five books Against Heresies, naming Rome's bishops in order down to his own day. His works sit on this tradition's Library shelf.
Most of these communities' hosts and householders are never named in the record. The gatherings met in their homes, but no record says whose.

Two enslaved women who served among these communities, called ministrae, are named only by their Roman interrogator's own word for their office — never by their own names. A governor had them tortured around the year 112 to learn what Christians did; it is the earliest outside evidence that women here held a formal title at all.
